name: Nomegestrol acetate

lead: Nomegestrol acetate is a prescription progestin used with estradiol in the Zoely contraceptive pill and alone for some gynaecological conditions. It is sold in Europe and Australia but not the US.
It has mild antiandrogenic activity, so acne improvement is suggested in reference works, but no acne trials were found.

paras: It selectively activates the progesterone receptor to suppress ovulation and has weak androgen receptor blocking activity.

Reported effects are typically mild: irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. Prolonged use at therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies. Prescription-only.

lead: Nomegestrol acetate (NOMAC) is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-norprogesterone. It is a potent, selective progesterone receptor agonist that suppresses ovulation and has some antiandrogenic activity, with no important androgenic, estrogenic, glucocorticoid or antimineralocorticoid effects.[1][2] It is used in combination with estradiol as a contraceptive pill (Zoely), for menopausal hormone therapy, and alone for certain gynaecological conditions (Lutenyl).[1][2]

In the appearance context, Wikipedia states that its antiandrogenic activity may help with acne, seborrhea and other androgen-dependent symptoms in women.[1] No acne-specific trial was among the sources reviewed, and Grokipedia lists acne among reported side effects of the drug.[2]

It is approved in Europe and Australia but not in the United States or Canada; the US FDA rejected the Zoely application in 2011.[1][2] Prolonged use of therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies.[2]
infobox: Prescription-only; not available in US or Canada

paras: The only appearance-related use found in the sources is the suggestion in Wikipedia that its antiandrogenic activity may benefit acne and seborrhea.[1] It is not marketed for acne.

NOMAC 2.5 mg with 1.5 mg estradiol (Zoely, 24 active tablets and 4 placebo) is a combined oral contraceptive approved in Europe in 2011 and Australia in 2012.[2] Alone it is used for menstrual disturbances, breast pain and uterine bleeding, and with estradiol in menopausal therapy; in France it is no longer recommended for menopausal hormone therapy as of 2023 because of meningioma risk.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes side effects as similar to other progestogens and usually mild: menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea and breast tenderness.[1] Grokipedia also lists acne, weight gain and irregular bleeding, and reports that use over a year at 3.75 to 5 mg has been associated with intracranial meningioma, with odds ratios up to 4.9 in epidemiological studies, and that MRI monitoring and contraindication in people with meningioma apply to therapeutic use.[2] Reviews of newer progestins discuss its pharmacological profile in contraception.[3][4][5]

NOMAC binds selectively to the progesterone receptor and exerts antigonadotropic effects; ovulation is suppressed at roughly 1.25 to 5 mg per day depending on the source and conditions.[1][2] It has some androgen receptor antagonism.[1] Wikipedia reports about 63 percent oral bioavailability, 97.5 to 98 percent protein binding, hepatic metabolism through CYP3A4 and a half-life near 50 hours.[1] Classification reviews place it among 19-norprogesterone derivatives.[6][7][8]

Nomegestrol was patented in 1975 and NOMAC (code TX-066) first described in 1983, developed by Theramex Laboratories of Monaco; Lutenyl and Naemis were introduced in Europe in 1986, and the Zoely contraceptive was approved in Europe in 2011.[1]

Brand names include Lutenyl, Naemis and Zoely.[1] It is prescription-only and available in much of Europe, Latin America and Asia-Pacific but not in the US or Canada.[1] No community discussion sources were reviewed for this entry.

Registered trials include a Phase 3 contraceptive efficacy and safety study of NOMAC-estradiol (terminated, about 3,000 participants), a large prospective cohort safety study of the 2.5 mg/1.5 mg pill in about 101,000 women, a pharmacokinetic study, a vaginal-ring dose-finding study, and a study of use in endometrial preparation.[9][10][11][12][13] A trial of postpartum relapse prevention in multiple sclerosis was also registered.[14] No acne trial was among them.
